The average size of micro-pores in the Ni-based single crystal superalloy is less than 30 μm, with a volume fraction less than 1%.
The number and volume fraction of micro-pores increase very slowly during the primary and secondary creep stages, but rapidly in the later stage of creep.
The number of solidification/hydrogen (S/H) pores shows little fluctuation until the very end of creep, then decreases rapidly due to the merging of neighboring pores.
The number of deformation (D) pores increases gradually, with the increasing rate becoming significant at the end of the secondary/beginning of the tertiary creep stage.
The shape factor of all micro-pores decreases in the late creep stage, indicating that the shape of all pores becomes more irregular as creep proceeds.
Plastic deformation rather than formation and growth of micro-pores is the main cause of creep strain in most of the creep life.
The final creep failure is resulted from the propagation of surface cracks induced by oxidation, and the internal cracks initiated from growth and connection of micro-pores.
The volume fraction of micro-pores increases after the creep strain, indicating that the increase in pore volume fraction is delayed compared to the increase in creep strain.
The rapid increase in strain rate coincides with the rapid growth of large pores, suggesting that the growth of large pores plays a dominant role in the creep damage at high temperature.
Micro-pores located in the strain concentration region, even if their sizes are not very large, can also significantly contribute to the creep damage due to their rapid growth and connection.
